transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-11-12 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Miguel Torres (Quantaco - Head of Infra), Sara Lin (Quantaco - ML Eng), Derek Park (Quantaco - CTO)

Summary (auto): Weekly POC check-in focusing on cost/unit economics; reviewed spreadsheet, discussed cache and batching tradeoffs; agreed benchmarking plan.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check in, we have about 45 minutes, main focus today is cost per unit and the caching/batching levers we talked about last week.
[00:12] Miguel Torres: Yep, thanks Alex. We have Derek and Sara here, want to make sure we understand what the real cost delta is before committing to more dedicated nodes.
[00:20] Priya Kapoor: Cool, I'll jump into the numbers after Alex goes through the sheet. Heads up, some of the metric names in the sheet are shorthand - tokens/sec/$ is tokens per second per dollar of instance cost, approx.
[00:33] Alex Chen: Right, so slide one, high level: hosted baseline using rXX-large GPU fleet — nominally our test shows ~1,200 tokens/sec on model-redwood-v1-quantized at batch=1, cost around $0.85/hr effective, which translates to tokens/sec/$ of about 1.4k. But that's without KV/prefix cache.
[00:50] Sara Lin: Can you repeat the tokens/sec/$ calc? We want units to map to our billing expectations.
[00:56] Alex Chen: Sure. tokens/sec divided by $/second. So 1,200 tokens/sec divided by $0.000236 per second (0.85/3600) ~= 5.08M tokens/sec per dollar, um wait—sorry brain slip, let me grab the sheet... the number in the sheet is 5.0M tokens per dollar for that config.
[01:18] Derek Park: That's helpful, but our primary metric is cost per 1M tokens for inference, not tokens/sec. How do these map?
[01:25] Priya Kapoor: You can invert it — 1 / (tokens per dollar / 1M) gives cost per 1M tokens. If it's 5M tokens per dollar, cost per 1M tokens is $0.20. But again that's baseline; caching can improve it substantially depending on prefix reuse.
[01:40] Miguel Torres: Right, and in our traffic a lot of requests share common prefixes — about 30% exact reuse per day. We ran a simple cache sim internally that suggested ~18-25% token savings.
[01:50] Alex Chen: Good, we ran a sim with KV cache enabled and saw effective token savings around 22% on their sample prompts which bumped tokens/sec/$ to ~6.4M, so cost per 1M tokens drops to ~$0.156.
[02:03] Sara Lin: Is that measured with batch size 1? Because batching could amplify throughput but hurts p95 latency.
[02:09] Priya Kapoor: The cache run was batch=1 to isolate cache effect. For batching, our estimates: batch=4 on the same model gives 3.8x throughput for many workloads but p95 latency increases by ~120-220ms depending on seq len. So tradeoff depends on your latency SLO.
[02:29] Derek Park: Our target is p95 < 350ms for synchronous features. If batch=4 pushes us above that for typical seq lengths, we can't rely on high batching in hosted mode.
[02:38] Alex Chen: Exactly; that's where dedicated capacity or model variant choices come in. With Dedicated we can reserve lower-overhead instances and tighter scheduling, getting similar throughput at lower cost per token because there's less queuing.
[02:50] Miguel Torres: Can you quantify that? How much lower?
[02:53] Priya Kapoor: In our previous benchmark, dedicated pool using A100 equivalent with tuned kernels and lower cos scheduling saw tokens/sec/$ bump of ~15-25% over the hosted baseline when you include autoscaling overheads removed. But the committed cost model means you pay fixed monthly for reserved capacity — good if you have steady load.
[03:12] Alex Chen: Also remember quantization profile affects both perf and quality. For quantized-8bit we saw ~10-15% perf gain on throughput but some customers need to validate quality. We included a quality monitor in the eval harness to compare perplexity/objective metrics.
[03:28] Sara Lin: Any quick notes on how caching interacts with quantization? Does KV content size change?
[03:33] Priya Kapoor: Cache stores key/value activations; quantization affects compute, not the cache footprint much, so the token savings % is roughly the same — the perf per token differs.
[03:43] Miguel Torres: Ok, what about real-world numbers — can we see a 24‑hour run with our traces?
[03:47] Alex Chen: Yes, that's in the action items. Priya will run a 24h tokens/sec benchmark with KV cache and batching combos using your 100k traces once you share them.
[03:56] Priya Kapoor: Plan is: run batch sizes 1, 4, 8 with cache off/on, capture tokens/sec, p50/p95 latencies, and per-token cost normalized to your committed rate. We'll also capture cold-starts and tail behavior.
[04:10] Derek Park: Also include a scenario where we force fallback to a cheaper model when cost threshold hit — we want to see graceful degradation.
[04:17] Alex Chen: We can simulate routing policies — fallback to smaller model for non-critical paths. We'll include warm/cold ratios.
[04:23] Sara Lin: A quick question: your sheet shows an optimistic cache saving of 35% in one row, but earlier numbers were ~22%. Which should we plan for?
[04:32] Priya Kapoor: The 35% row is an upper bound from a high-reuse traffic pattern. For Quantaco's sample traces you reported ~30% reuse, but effective token saving depends on where the reuse occurs in sequence. We're conservatively modeling 20-25% until the 24h runs confirm.
[04:45] Miguel Torres: Understood. On billing mapping, how do you recommend we think about committed Dedicated vs hosted metered for our expected QPS of ~150 qps?
[04:54] Alex Chen: If your steady working set is high and predictable at 150 qps with sustained long sessions, Dedicated likely lowers unit cost after amortizing reserved node fees. For bursty load, hosted with autoscaling plus an occasional dedicated buffer or burst policy is often better. We'll put a comparative table in the sheet with break-even points.
[05:12] Derek Park: Please include assumptions: avg seq len, tokens per request, cache hit rate.
[05:16] Alex Chen: Yep — the sheet has a assumptions section. For our baseline we used avg seq len 120 tokens, tokens per request 200 (including system tokens), cache hit 22% (conservative). We'll mark them clearly.
[05:30] Sara Lin: On security/compliance, if we move to Private, what's the overhead for us in terms of ops hours? We have to estimate total cost of ownership, not just tokens.
[05:39] Priya Kapoor: Good point — Private has setup and maintenance effort. We can provide a rough OPEX estimate (patching, KMS integration, monitoring) per year. We'll add that to the comparison table.
[05:48] Miguel Torres: Ok great. Anything else on the numbers?
[05:51] Alex Chen: Last thing — latency tail when batching is the main reason customers avoid large batch sizes for interactive features. For async workloads (embeddings, large batch rerank), batching is a big win. We'll separate those in the sheet.
[06:05] Derek Park: Sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[06:08] Alex Chen: Recap: Alex to share updated spreadsheet with break-even and assumptions by Friday 11/14; Priya to run 24h benchmark with cache on/off and batch sizes 1/4/8 using Quantaco sample traces, results by 11/18; Quantaco to confirm SLOs and provide sample traces by 11/15. Also potential separate thread to schedule private deployment deep dive.
[06:29] Miguel Torres: Thanks much. We'll get the traces over today.
[06:32] Sara Lin: I'll upload the 100k sample and a small runbook of our traffic shape.
[06:36] Alex Chen: Perfect — thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the sheet and the bench plan.
[06:41] Derek Park: Thanks all.
[06:42] (call ends)

Notes: minor transcription errors present (e.g., KV cache sometimes transcribed as KV cash). References to shared doc: https://redwood.internal/pocecon/CRM-78942 (sheet).
